info.bio: Bruce Cockburn (pronounced "CO-burn") (born May 27, 1945 in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada) has had a long and distinguished career, with much success in his native Canada. He has written songs in styles ranging from folk to jazz-influenced rock to rock and roll. Cockburn was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 2001. In 2012 he received the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal (in Canada the award was to honour "significant contributions and achievements by Canadians").

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.title: 1986 Alt-Rock Radio Playlists
podcast.body: Bruce Cockburn (referred to as "Bruce Cogrid" in the transcript) was featured on alt-rock radio playlists in the mid-1980s, demonstrating the inclusion of "modern focus" artists alongside a wide range of other genres. "There was mainstream stuff, like invisible touch from Genesis, and modern focus stuff from people like Bruce Cogrid."

podcast.title: Emergence as Serious Stars
podcast.body: Bruce Cockburn emerged as one of the serious stars through the late 1970s and into the 1980s, benefiting from the new industry infrastructure and increased radio support for Canadian talent. This period marked a shift towards greater national and international success for homegrown artists. "Love her boy, Chilla Wack, Bruce Coburn, rough trade, the pay-all was Toronto, the headpins, the spoons, bride-adams, parachute club, men without hats, Cory Hart. They all emerged as serious stars through the late 1970s and into the 1980s."

podcast.title: True North Records Success
podcast.body: Bruce Cockburn was one of the artists on True North Records who, thanks to Cancon quotas, "broke through and had legitimate hits," contributing to the label's success. "True North was unabashedly Canadian, and thanks to the Cancon quotas, a few of their acts broke through and had legitimate hits, artists like Bruce Cobard in Rough Trade."

xref.title: Admiration from Renowned Artists
xref.body: O'Hara garnered significant praise and admiration from many influential musicians; Morrissey requested her for vocalizations on his single "November Spawned a Demon," and Michael Stipe of R.E.M., Radiohead, Bruce Cockburn, Dave Matthews, and Nick Cave were all noted fans of her distinct music. "Moresy was such a fan that he asked her to do some vocalizations on his single November Spawn Demonstrer. Michael Steip couldn't get enough of her. Radiohead, Bruce Coburn, Dave Matthews, Nick Cave, they were all fans."

xref.title: Early Electric Guitar Influences
xref.body: Ian Thornley quickly acquired an electric guitar, a delay pedal, and a whammy bar, eager to emulate his influences. He was particularly obsessed with Bruce Cockburn's song "If a Tree Falls" and also practiced U2's music, using the gear to achieve similar sounds. "I was obsessed with if a tree falls or, yeah, if a tree falls. And that that, he used the whammy bar and the delay pedal."
